item.title: wp2shell, ServiceNow CVE-2026-6875, and Langflow RCE Drive Active Exploitation
item.content:encoded:
WordPress wp2shell Exploitation Grows as Public Exploit Fuels Mass Scanning — Must Read

Attackers are widely exploiting the wp2shell WordPress vulnerability chain to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on vulnerable sites, with mass scanning and post-exploitation activity including malicious plugins, web shells, and backdoor admin accounts. Defenders should patch immediately and inspect even patched sites for signs of compromise.

  • Attackers have begun exploiting two critical WordPress vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137, together under the name wp2shell to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution and compromise vulnerable websites.
  • KEVIntel telemetry linked exploitation of CVE-2026-63030 to 13 unique IP addresses from Switzerland, Germany, the U.K., Indonesia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, and Singapore.
  • Cloudflare said CVE-2026-63030 enables unauthenticated remote code execution only when persistent object cache is not in use, while CVE-2026-60137 is present from WordPress version 6.8 onward and the RCE affects versions from 6.9.
  • Wiz observed post-exploitation activity including malicious plugin uploads, user enumeration, local file inclusion attacks targeting database credentials and authentication keys, admin panel access, and PHP web shell uploads.
  • WatchTowr said public exploit release led attackers to scan the internet indiscriminately, with honeypots registering tens of thousands of exploitation attempts and more than 100 backdoor administrator accounts created after exploitation.

Critical ServiceNow AI Platform Flaw Exploited for Unauthenticated Code Execution — Must Read

Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2026-6875, a critical pre-authentication sandbox escape flaw in ServiceNow AI Platform that can allow unauthenticated arbitrary code execution and full instance compromise. Self-hosted ServiceNow customers should apply the June patches immediately.

  • Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-6875, a critical sandbox escape vulnerability in the ServiceNow AI Platform, according to Defused Cyber.
  • CVE-2026-6875 has a CVSS score of 9.5 and could allow an unauthenticated user to run arbitrary code.
  • ServiceNow released patches for the flaw throughout June in Brazil EA and GA, Australia Patch 2, Zurich Patch 7b and Patch 9, and Yokohama Patch 12 Hot Fix 1b and Patch 13.
  • Searchlight Cyber said it reported the issue on April 1, 2026, and that the flaw allows complete compromise of the ServiceNow instance and all connected proxy servers.
  • Defused Cyber said exploitation efforts target the pre-authentication endpoint “/assessment_thanks.do” using HTTP POST requests.

New ENCFORGE Ransomware Targets AI Model Files in Langflow RCE Attack — Must Read

A threat actor tracked as JADEPUFFER is exploiting an unauthenticated Langflow RCE flaw to deploy ENCFORGE, a new Go-based ransomware built to encrypt AI model weights, vector indexes, and training datasets. Organizations should urgently patch Langflow, rotate exposed credentials, remove unnecessary Docker socket access, and keep immutable backups of AI assets.

  • Sysdig linked a second attack on the same Langflow server to JADEPUFFER, an AI-agent-driven operator previously documented earlier in the month.
  • The attacker deployed ENCFORGE, a new compiled Go ransomware designed to encrypt AI-related files such as model weights, vector indexes, training datasets, PyTorch and TensorFlow checkpoints, SafeTensors, ONNX, GGUF, FAISS indexes, Parquet, Arrow, NumPy arrays, and TensorFlow records.
  • The entry point was CVE-2025-3248, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Langflow versions before 1.3.0 affecting the /api/v1/validate/code endpoint.
  • After finding the Docker socket at /var/run/docker.sock, the operator created and revised six Python scripts through Langflow RCE to launch a privileged container, mount the host filesystem, copy ENCFORGE to the host, and run it with nsenter.
  • The article recommends upgrading Langflow to 1.9.1 or a current supported release, rotating credentials accessible to Langflow, removing unnecessary Docker socket access, alerting on privileged container behavior, and keeping model artifacts in offline or immutable snapshots.

New Project CAV3RN module abuses Outlook calendar events for C2 and DNS AAAA records for configuration recovery — Should Read

Kaspersky analyzed a new Project CAV3RN communication module that replaces traditional C2 with Microsoft Graph access to hidden Outlook calendar events for commands, results, and heartbeats. If Microsoft Graph access fails, the module can recover updated tenant, app, secret, and mailbox settings through actor-controlled DNS AAAA records, reinforcing the assessment that the OilRig-linked framework remains actively developed.

  • Kaspersky identified a .NET Native AOT communication module named AzureCommunication.dll that appears designed to replace Project CAV3RN’s previous HTTP/WebSocket communication component.
  • The module exchanges commands, heartbeats, and command results through Outlook calendar events accessed via Microsoft Graph in the default calendar of a configured mailbox.
  • Commands and results are stored as encrypted calendar event attachments using RSA-OAEP with SHA-256 and AES-256-GCM, with events placed in a fixed one-hour window on May 13, 2050.
  • If Microsoft Graph authentication or organization validation fails, the module attempts to recover replacement TenantId, ClientId, ClientSecret, and UserEmail values through DNS AAAA responses from cloudlanecdn.com.
  • Kaspersky retains a low-confidence assessment that Project CAV3RN is associated with OilRig based on behavioral similarities such as use of Microsoft-hosted services, attachment-based command exchange, and a secondary mechanism for restoring cloud C2 access.

Windows LegacyHive zero-day flaw gets free, unofficial patches — Should Read

Free unofficial 0patch micropatches are available for the Windows LegacyHive zero-day, which lets non-admin users gain access to other users’ registry hives and potentially escalate privileges. Microsoft is still investigating and has not yet issued an official patch or CVE.

  • Free unofficial patches are available from ACROS Security’s 0Patch platform for the Windows LegacyHive zero-day flaw.
  • LegacyHive was disclosed by a researcher using the handle Nightmare Eclipse and affects the Windows User Profile Service.
  • The vulnerability allows a regular non-admin user to mount another user’s registry hive with full access, potentially extracting stored secrets or changing registry values that affect what runs when that user next logs in.
  • Microsoft said it is aware of the reported vulnerability and is actively investigating its validity and potential applicability.
  • ACROS Security provides micropatches for Windows 10 2004 or later and Windows Server 2022 or later, and says the flaw does not affect Windows versions older than Windows 10 2004 and Windows Server 2019.

Microsoft shares manual fix for WSUS sync delays and timeouts — Should Read

Microsoft provided manual cleanup steps for existing WSUS servers still suffering from synchronization delays and timeouts caused by excess publishing metadata. Admins should back up SUSDB, run Microsoft’s cleanup query, reindex and clean up WSUS, then reset IIS or recycle WsusPool to restore normal update scans.

  • Microsoft shared manual mitigations for Windows Server Update Services servers affected by a known issue that causes Windows Update scans to fail or time out.
  • The issue affects Windows 10 version 1607 and later, as well as Windows Server 2012 and later, and can prevent admins from deploying the latest Windows updates through WSUS or Configuration Manager.
  • Microsoft said synchronization times and operations have been restored for new WSUS installations and rebuilds after a service-side mitigation was rolled out.
  • For existing affected WSUS installations, Microsoft recommends backing up each SUSDB database, running a cleanup query against all SUSDB databases, and resetting MaxXMLPerRequest to its default setting.
  • After cleanup, Microsoft says administrators should reindex SUSDB, run the WSUS Server Cleanup Wizard, and run IISReset or recycle the WsusPool application pool to clear cached catalog state.

When Production Stops Anyway — May Read

The Fairlife ransomware incident shows that food and beverage production can be forced to stop even without confirmed OT compromise, because plants depend on IT systems for traceability, quality release, scheduling, and logistics. The key lesson is that manufacturers need clear visibility and segmentation across IT and plant environments so they can make evidence-based shutdown and restart decisions.

  • The Coca-Cola Company disclosed on 16 July that its dairy subsidiary Fairlife detected unauthorised access to part of its systems, including production-related systems, in connection with a ransomware attack.
  • Production across Fairlife’s US operations was temporarily suspended, while Canadian operations were not affected and product quality and safety were reported as unimpacted.
  • The article states that there is no public confirmation that the attackers reached Fairlife’s OT network, but production stopped anyway because food and beverage manufacturing depends on systems for scheduling, recipe management, quality release, traceability, labelling, and logistics.
  • The article argues that if a ransomware incident casts doubt on the integrity of traceability records or takes them offline, stopping production is the only defensible decision in a regulated food environment.
  • The article says food and beverage manufacturers should understand which IT systems production depends on, maintain visibility into plant networks and their connections, and use segmentation and separation to support incident response decisions.
